As far as when to use growth rates, there's no definitive answer as it depends on the objectives of your analysis. You should consider using growth rates when the magnitudes of the variables don't matter as much as their relative changes, when you want to ensure stationarity, and when you're interested in examining the proportional effect of one variable on another. The quicksort algorithm is a divide-and-conquer algorithm used for sorting a list of elements. While there is a focus on its time complexity, its space complexity is also significant.

In terms of its spatial complexity, quicksort performs quite well since it does not require any extra space besides the array itself and some for the recursive calls.

1. Best Case Space Complexity - O(log n): 

   The best case happens when the partition process always picks the middle element as pivot. The minumum depth of recursive tree is log(n) and each level of tree needs O(1) space, thus the space complexity is O(log n). 

2. Average Case Space Complexity - O(log n): 

   On average, quicksort has a space complexity of O(log n) for the call stack during recursion, which holds the intermediate values during the partitioning process. This is because each recursive call processes a list that is half the size of the previous one, creating a binary recursion tree.

3. Worst Case Space Complexity - O(N): 

   The worst case happens when the partition process always picks greatest or smallest element as pivot. If the partitioning phase of quicksort does not divide the array in approximately half, for the case where partition gives two sub-arrays of the size of N-1 and 1, then each recursive step will add a new level to the call stack, ending in O(n) extra space.

Though, we can optimize the space by tail recursion or eliminating tail recursion to bring back the space complexity to O(log n).

These complexities are considering an in-place sort where the sorting operation is performed without the use of any extra memory; hence, the spatial complexity is relatively minimal.

However, it's crucial to remember that this Big O notation analysis is an approximation, which is suitable when considering large data-sets. For smaller data-sets, the space complexity may not be significant.
